https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12045.what_the_source_says: τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024) is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in two real-world domains (retail and airline), where a simulated user and an LLM agent with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines converse, and success is judged by comparing the end-of-conversation database state to an annotated goal state. The paper's stated concern is that it is not enough to build agents with high average, one-shot success (pass^1) — it also proposes pass^k as a new metric for measuring reliability/consistency across repeated trials on the same task, distinct from the pre-existing pass@k metric (probability of at least one success across k attempts). The paper reports that even GPT-4o-based function-calling agents succeed on under 50% of tasks and are 'terribly inconsistent' (pass^8 < 25% in retail), which is offered as evidence that capability and reliability are different things.

https://buttondown.com/hillelwayne/archi.what_the_source_says: Hillel Wayne's newsletter post distinguishes a 'weak version' of Goodhart's law (people have perverse incentives to game a metric once it's a target — e.g., if the metric is 'number of bugs in the bug tracker,' people start spuriously closing bugs, splitting a bug into multiple tickets to inflate closure counts, or prioritizing trivial bugs over complex ones) from a 'strong version' (even fully honest pursuit of a metric, taken far enough, becomes harmful — illustrated with the biological example of peahen plumage becoming a sexual-selection target at the cost of overall bird fitness). On test coverage specifically, the post's point (per search results) is that a target of e.g. 95% coverage causes trivial tests that don't validate real logic, and that coverage alone is close to meaningless as a quality signal. Wayne also cites a counter-example he considers hard to game: Keith Braithwaite's metric of the slope of method-complexity vs. number-of-methods, which correlated with whether a codebase had real unit-test/TDD discipline.

https://philschmid.de/agents-pass-at-k-p.what_the_source_says: Philipp Schmid's personal blog post 'Pass@k vs Pass^k: Understanding Agent Reliability' explains, in plain language, that pass@k measures 'the probability that at least one of k independent solution attempts will succeed' (a standard metric already used in code-generation benchmarks), while pass^k ('pass power k') measures the probability that ALL k attempts succeed, and falls as k increases — his framing is that pass@k describes peak/best-case capability while pass^k describes production reliability/consistency. He illustrates the practical stakes with a customer-support/airline-rebooking example (three consecutive rebooking requests only succeeding together 34.3% of the time) and gives a decision rule: use pass@k when a human reviews every output (human-in-the-loop), use pass^k when output is consumed automatically (e.g. merging code, sending messages, modifying databases) because consistency across all attempts matters there.

https://getdx.com/research/measuring-dev.what_the_source_says: DX's Core 4 framework (from getdx.com, DX being Laura Tacho and Abi Noda's company) defines four counterbalanced dimensions — Speed, Effectiveness, Quality, Impact — combining ideas from DORA, SPACE, and DevEx research. 'Diffs per engineer' (or PRs per engineer) is the primary Speed metric, explicitly intended as an aggregate/team/organizational-level snapshot of flow, not a per-person score; search results describe an explicit caveat/asterisk in the framework reading approximately 'not to measure this at the individual level' and state it should never be tied to performance evaluations. Effectiveness is measured via the Developer Experience Index (DXI), a 14-item Likert-scale survey score, which the framework uses as a counterbalance so that a focus on raw throughput (diffs) doesn't dominate the picture; Quality uses Change Failure Rate, and Impact uses percentage of time spent on new capabilities.
